short.content: Sunlight enters the Earth's atmosphere and is scattered by gas molecules, a phenomenon known as Rayleigh scattering. This scattering process affects shorter wavelengths of light more strongly than longer ones, causing blue light to be dispersed in all directions across the sky. Consequently, when we look up, our eyes detect this abundant scattered blue light, making the sky appear blue rather than white or black.

The wind off the North Sea did not howl; it screamed. It was a high, thin shriek that tore through the gaps in the stone masonry of the lighthouse, vibrating in Elias’s teeth. He had been keeping the light for three years, long enough to know the rhythm of the storm, but this one felt different. It felt personal. The rain lashed against the curved glass of the lantern room, blurring the horizon into a churning gray smear where water and sky lost all distinction.

Elias wiped the condensation from the lens with a rag that had grown stiff from salt and age. His hands were mapped with scars, pale lines crossing over knuckles swollen by decades of cold work. He was tired. Not just physically, though his back ached with every step up the spiral staircase, but a deeper, bone-weariness that settled in his marrow. He missed the quiet of the mainland, the smell of baked bread, the silence that wasn’t punctuated by the relentless crash of waves against the rocks below.

While checking the oil reserves, he noticed a draft near the base of the lamp housing. A loose panel of wood, rotted at the edges, hung open like a mouth trying to speak. Curiosity, a dangerous companion for a solitary man, pulled him toward it. He pried the panel free. Behind it, tucked into a cavity that should have been solid stone, lay a leather-bound book.

It was thick, its cover cracked and faded to the color of dried blood. The spine was held together with fraying wire. Elias picked it up. It was heavy, dense with history. He opened it carefully, fearing the pages might disintegrate into dust. The ink was brown, faded by time and moisture, but still legible. The handwriting was jagged, hurried, written by someone who was terrified.

*Day 42,* the first entry read. *The light is failing. I have tried everything. The wick burns unevenly. The keeper on rotation says we must wait for the supply boat, but the sea will not let them pass. I am alone now. The last one left three days ago. He said he would return. He did not.*

Elias frowned. He knew the logs of this lighthouse. They were meticulous, precise records of weather patterns and maintenance schedules. There was no mention of abandonment or failure. He turned the page.

*Day 50. The storms are worse than I imagined. They do not just break the waves; they seem to reach out. I saw something in the water today. Not a whale. Not a shark. Something with eyes that reflected the beam. It watched me until I cut the power. When I restored it, it was gone. But I hear scratching on the outside of the door. All night. Scratching and whispering.*

A chill that had nothing to do with the winter air crept up Elias’s spine. He looked out the window. The darkness beyond the glass was absolute, save for the occasional flash of lightning that illuminated the black water. For a second, he thought he saw a shape moving in the surf, vast and dark, breaking the surface before sinking back down. He blinked, and it was gone.

He continued reading. The entries grew shorter, more frantic. The handwriting slanted further right, as if the writer was losing control of their own hand.

*Day 61. I cannot sleep. If I close my eyes, I see the face. It has no features, only a smooth, wet surface. It presses against the glass. I am afraid to look away. I am afraid to look at it. I am going to stay in the lantern room. I will keep the light on. If the light goes out, it comes in. I don’t know why. I don’t understand. But I know it is true.*

The final entry was just a single word, scrawled so hard the pen had torn the paper: *Help.*

There were no more pages. Just blankness.

Elias sat on the cold stone floor, the logbook resting on his knees. The wind howled louder, rattling the windows. He looked at the massive Fresnel lens, towering above him, refracting the flame into a powerful beam that swept across the treacherous waters. It was a beacon of safety, or so he had always believed. But looking at the logbook, the narrative shifted. Was the light a warning? Or was it a lure?

He remembered the stories the fishermen told in the pub on the mainland. Stories about ships that vanished without a trace, drawn into the fog and never seen again. They called it the Devil’s Pull. They said the light didn’t guide you home; it guided you to your grave.

def is_palindrome(s):
    cleaned = ''.join(c.lower() for c in s if c.isalnum())
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]
